title: Dene Company eyeglass frames: FIFO vs. LIFO ending inventory and cost of goods sold (periodic system)
participant_role: New accountant at Dene Company, a maker of molded eyeglass frames
judge_role: Manager of Dene Company who wants to switch inventory costing methods each year to maximize profit
scenario:
You are to assume the role of the new accountant at DENE COMPANY, a company that molds materials into eyeglass frames. The company manager (judge) wants you to calculate ending inventory and cost of goods sold.

The company is reporting the following for the month of October:

October 1 Inventory: 200 units at $5 unit cost, $1,000 total cost
October 12 Purchases: 300 units at $6 unit cost, $1,800 total cost
October 23 Purchases: 500 units at $7 unit cost, $3,500 total cost
October 31 Inventory: 180 units

The manager (judge) understands inventory costing can be calculated using several accepted methods but wants what is right for the company and proposes to vary the inventory costing methods annually to maximize profits.

The manager (judge) wants to discuss the inventory numbers and relative inventory costing. The manager (judge) has asked you to calculate the ending inventory and the cost of goods sold using a periodic inventory system under FIFO and LIFO. You will also calculate which costing method gives a higher ending inventory and explain why. The manager (judge) wants you to explain why a company is not allowed to change the inventory costing method regularly to benefit net income.

You will present the information to the manager (judge) in a role-play to take place in the manager's (judge's) office. The manager (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the manager's (judge's) questions, the manager (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

solution.overview: A strong answer first shows cost of goods available for sale of $6,300 for 1,000 units, with 820 units sold and 180 left. Under FIFO, COGS is $5,040 and ending inventory is $1,260; under LIFO, COGS is $5,400 and ending inventory is $900. FIFO gives the higher ending inventory because costs are rising and the newest, most expensive units stay in inventory. The company must pick one method and apply it consistently; switching every year to boost net income violates the consistency principle and is an ethics breach under GAAP and IFRS.

answer: Goods available for sale: 200 + 300 + 500 = 1,000 units costing $1,000 + $1,800 + $3,500 = $6,300
Units sold: 1,000 available less 180 ending = 820 units
Check: COGS + ending inventory = $6,300 under both methods ($5,040 + $1,260 and $5,400 + $900)

by_task.task: Which method gives higher ending inventory and why
answer: FIFO gives the higher ending inventory: $1,260 versus $900 under LIFO
Costs rose during October from $5 to $7 per unit
FIFO assigns the earliest (cheapest) costs to cost of goods sold, so the latest (most expensive) costs remain in ending inventory
Because FIFO COGS is lower ($5,040 vs. $5,400), FIFO also reports $360 more gross profit this month

by_task.task: Why the method cannot be changed regularly
answer: GAAP permits a choice of method, but the best method is the one that most fairly matches costs against the sales revenue of the period
The consistency principle requires the same method year after year so financial statements are comparable
Switching methods just to manage net income misleads banks, investors and tax authorities and is considered a breach of ethics under GAAP and IFRS
A change is allowed only when justified and must be disclosed in the notes, with the effect on income shown
Note that LIFO is not allowed under IFRS at all

steps: Ending inventory: FIFO $1,260 - LIFO $900 = $360 higher under FIFO
COGS: LIFO $5,400 - FIFO $5,040 = $360 higher under LIFO
Gross profit is therefore $360 higher under FIFO in a rising-cost period

judge_question_answers.question: Why is it important to maintain inventory records?
answer: Inventory is an asset on the balance sheet and its cost drives cost of goods sold and net income, so errors flow straight into the financial statements and taxes
Records tell management what to reorder and when, preventing stockouts and overstocking of frame materials
They help detect theft, damage and shrinkage when the physical count is compared to the records
Auditors, lenders and the IRS expect supported inventory figures

judge_question_answers.question: What can affect inventory numbers besides purchases and sales?
answer: Shrinkage: theft, breakage, spoilage or damage to materials and frames
Purchase returns to suppliers and customer returns coming back into stock
Counting or recording errors, and items in transit or on consignment at period end
Obsolete or defective units written down to market value

key_concepts.definition: Inventory is counted at the end of the period and cost of goods sold is figured then: Beginning inventory + Purchases - Ending inventory = COGS.

key_concepts.term: Cost of goods available for sale
key_concepts.definition: Beginning inventory plus all purchases for the period; it is split between ending inventory and cost of goods sold.
Assumes the oldest costs are sold first, so ending inventory holds the newest costs. In rising prices FIFO gives lower COGS, higher ending inventory and higher profit.
Assumes the newest costs are sold first, so ending inventory holds the oldest costs. In rising prices LIFO gives higher COGS, lower ending inventory and lower profit (and lower taxes).
Total cost of goods available divided by total units available gives one average unit cost applied to both COGS and ending inventory (here $6,300 / 1,000 = $6.30 per unit).
The cost of the inventory actually sold during the period; Sales - COGS = Gross profit.
The cost assigned to the units still on hand at period end; reported as a current asset on the balance sheet.
A company should use the same accounting methods from period to period so its statements can be compared; changes must be justified and disclosed.
Expenses (including COGS) should be recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped earn.
A situation where a manager wants to use an allowed choice, such as switching inventory methods, mainly to make results look better; the accountant must follow GAAP and refuse to manipulate income.
The difference between recorded inventory and the physical count caused by theft, damage, spoilage or errors.
